3.4 Interest Rate Risk

Two kinds of interest rate risk

Section titled “Two kinds of interest rate risk”

Even if a bond does not default, changes in interest rates change how much money the investor ends up with. 3.3 Bond Pricing showed two effects:

  • Price risk: when rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall. Selling before maturity then means a loss.
  • Reinvestment risk: when rates fall, coupons and principal received can only be reinvested at lower rates.

The two risks work in opposite directions: when rates rise, prices suffer but reinvestment gains; when rates fall, the reverse. For an investor with a fixed horizon, very short bonds carry mainly reinvestment risk and very long bonds mainly price risk. Can one choose a maturity at which the two offset each other? To answer this we need a measure of sensitivity to interest rates.

Check C1
An investor will need some money in 5 years. Just after he buys, rates fall sharply and stay low. Which approach ends up better than originally expected?
The investor rolling 1-year bills must reinvest each year at the rate of the time. After rates fall, does he earn more or less?
The two approaches face risks in opposite directions, so one move in rates cannot help both.
The two approaches face risks in opposite directions, so one move in rates cannot hurt both.

Duration

Section titled “Duration”

Write a bond’s cash flow in year ttt as CFt\text{CF}_tCFt​, its yield as yyy and its price as PPP. The shares of the price contributed by each cash flow’s present value, wt=CFt/(1+y)tPw_t = \frac{\text{CF}_t / (1 + y)^t}{P}wt​=PCFt​/(1+y)t​, add up to 1. Averaging the times of the cash flows with these shares as weights gives the Macaulay duration:

D=∑t=1Tt wtD = \sum_{t=1}^{T} t \, w_tD=t=1∑T​twt​

It is the average time to receive cash, weighted by present value. A zero-coupon bond has a single cash flow, so its duration equals its maturity; a coupon bond receives part of its cash earlier, so its duration is shorter than its maturity. The higher the coupon rate or the yield, the more weight on early cash flows and the shorter the duration; the longer the maturity, the longer the duration, in general.

Duration matters because it measures how sensitive the price is to the yield. Differentiating the price gives (Exercises Question 1):

ΔPP≈−D∗ Δy,D∗=D1+y\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \, \Delta y, \qquad D^* = \frac{D}{1 + y}PΔP​≈−D∗Δy,D∗=1+yD​

D∗D^*D∗ is called the modified duration: when the yield changes by 1 percentage point, the price changes by about D∗D^*D∗ percent in the opposite direction. For example, a bond fund with a modified duration of 7 loses about 7% of its value if rates rise by 1 percentage point.

Check C2
At the same yield, among all Treasuries maturing in 10 years, the 10-year zero-coupon bond's price is the most sensitive to changes in yield.
Think: among Treasuries maturing in 10 years, which one returns its cash latest on average? How is duration related to price sensitivity?

Convexity

Section titled “Convexity”

Duration approximates the relation between price and yield with a straight line, but 3.3 Bond Pricing showed that the relation is a convex curve. For larger yield changes, the error of the straight line cannot be ignored. A correction with the second derivative gives

ΔPP≈−D∗ Δy+12 C (Δy)2\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \, \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} \, C \, (\Delta y)^2PΔP​≈−D∗Δy+21​C(Δy)2

CCC is called convexity, C=1Pd2Pdy2C = \frac{1}{P} \frac{d^2 P}{d y^2}C=P1​dy2d2P​. For ordinary bonds C>0C > 0C>0, so the second term is always positive: when the yield falls the price rises more than duration predicts, and when it rises the price falls less. For the same duration, more convexity is better for the investor; so the market generally also accepts a lower yield for more convexity (Exercises Question 5).

Check C3
In Figure 3-1, fix the change in yield at a 2-point rise and lengthen the bond's maturity from 10 to 30 years. The gap between the duration estimate and the exact price change:
As maturity lengthens, does the price curve bend more or less? What happens to the error of a straight-line approximation?
The same change in yield affects bonds of different maturities differently; the error of the duration estimate depends on how much the price curve bends.

Immunization

Section titled “Immunization”

Suppose a fixed payment is due in 5 years (a debt, say, or a child’s tuition) and bonds are bought today to prepare for it. If the bond portfolio has a Macaulay duration of 5 years, then after a one-time change in rates, the change in price and the change in reinvestment income move in opposite directions by about the same amount, and the portfolio’s value in year 5 is roughly unaffected. This is called immunization. The conditions: the present value of the assets equals that of the liability, and the duration of the assets equals that of the liability.

The simplest way is to buy a 5-year zero. Without a suitable zero, one can combine bonds of different maturities; the duration of a portfolio is the value-weighted average of the bonds’ durations.

Immunization has limits:

  • both the passage of time and rate changes alter durations, so the portfolio must be rebalanced regularly to keep its duration equal to the time remaining;
  • it holds only approximately for parallel shifts of the whole yield curve and can fail when short and long rates change differently;
  • the liability’s convexity should be lower than the assets’, or large rate changes create a shortfall.

This idea also matters for the bank risk of 2.3 Money and Banking: a bank’s assets (long-term loans, bonds) have long durations and its liabilities (deposits) short ones, so when rates rise the value of its assets falls more than that of its liabilities, and shareholders’ equity suffers (Exercises Question 4).

Check C4
A fixed amount must be paid in 5 years. Which portfolio (each worth today the present value of the liability) comes closest to immunization?
Rolling 1-year bills has a very short duration and bears mainly reinvestment risk: if rates fall, the money in 5 years falls short of the liability.
A 30-year bond has a duration far longer than 5 years and bears mainly price risk: if rates rise, selling after 5 years means a loss.
The same maturity date does not mean the same duration. A bond with a very high coupon returns much of its cash early; is its duration 5 years?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Rate changes bring price risk and reinvestment risk, in opposite directions.
  • Macaulay duration D=∑tt wtD = \sum_t t \, w_tD=∑t​twt​ is the present-value-weighted average time to receive cash; a zero’s duration equals its maturity. Modified duration D∗=D1+yD^* = \frac{D}{1 + y}D∗=1+yD​, and ΔPP≈−D∗Δy\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \Delta yPΔP​≈−D∗Δy.
  • Convexity corrects the error of duration: ΔPP≈−D∗Δy+12C(Δy)2\frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} C (\Delta y)^2PΔP​≈−D∗Δy+21​C(Δy)2; more convexity is better for the holder.
  • Immunization: equal present values and durations of assets and liabilities make the price and reinvestment effects of a one-time rate change offset; it needs regular rebalancing and holds only approximately for parallel shifts.

Question 3 ★
10,000 is due in 5 years, 7835.26 is available today, and the yield curve is flat at 5%. An adviser says: "Rates may change, so the safest approach is to roll 1-year zeros every year; short-term bonds have no interest rate risk." Suppose that right after buying, yields shift down in parallel to 3% and stay there. Compare how much each approach has in year 5: (i) roll 1-year zeros every year; (ii) buy a 10-year zero and sell it in year 5; (iii) half in a 2-year zero and half in an 8-year zero, reinvesting maturing money at the prevailing rate and selling the remaining bond in year 5. Which approach comes closest to 10,000? Why? What is wrong with the adviser's statement?

(a) Use modified duration to estimate the change in equity. (b) With Silicon Valley Bank from 2.3 Money and Banking in mind, explain why such a duration gap can put a bank with no bad loans into crisis.
